title: Creatine May Supercharge Immune Cells That Fight Cancer, UCLA Study Finds
excerpt: The popular fitness supplement energized dendritic cells that direct the body's cancer-killing T cells, slowing tumor growth in mice and pointing to potential applications in immunotherapy and cancer vaccines.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Creatine boosts dendritic cells, enhancing their ability to direct T cells against tumors.
  • Daily creatine injections slowed tumor growth in melanoma mouse models and activated immune cells.
  • The supplement shows promise for improving cancer vaccines and existing immunotherapies.
  • Creatine supplementation energized dendritic cells — immune cells that direct T cells to attack tumors — by boosting their ATP energy levels, according to UCLA researchers.
  • Daily creatine injections significantly slowed tumor growth in mouse models of melanoma and increased the number and activation of tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells.
  • The supplement also enhanced human dendritic cell activation in lab tests, suggesting potential applications in cancer vaccine manufacturing and as a complement to existing immunotherapies.

Creatine, the organic acid that bodybuilders and athletes swear by for muscle recovery, may have a far more consequential role: supercharging the immune cells that direct the body's fight against cancer.

Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles published findings in iScience showing that creatine fuels dendritic cells — specialized immune sentinels that capture tumor fragments and direct killer T cells to attack. The study, conducted in mouse models and human cells, builds on the team's earlier work demonstrating that creatine powers T cells in their battle against tumors.

How It Works

The research team, led by Lili Yang, a professor of microbiology, immunology and molecular genetics at UCLA, began by mapping which metabolic genes were most active in dendritic cells that had infiltrated tumors in mice. They found that the gene encoding the creatine transporter — a protein that pulls creatine inside cells — was markedly elevated in dendritic cells inside tumors compared to those in healthy tissue.

To test the significance, the team engineered dendritic cells that lacked the creatine transporter entirely. These cells showed impaired survival, reduced activation, and a weakened ability to prime T cells. When creatine-deficient dendritic cells were grown alongside T cells in a lab dish, the T cells divided less and produced fewer of the signaling molecules needed to fight cancer.

"What this study shows is that creatine doesn't just help the T cells fighting cancer — it also energizes the entire infrastructure that supports and guides them."

— Lili Yang, UCLA

Slowing Tumor Growth

The opposite intervention produced encouraging results. Daily creatine injections in mouse models of melanoma significantly slowed tumor growth and boosted both the abundance and activation of tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells. The creatine-treated cells also produced higher levels of chemical signals that draw additional immune cells into tumors.

Using metabolomics analyses, the researchers found that creatine raised intracellular ATP levels in dendritic cells — ATP is the energy currency cells use to power virtually every function. Like a rechargeable battery, creatine helped dendritic cells maintain stable energy levels even when competing with fast-growing tumor cells for nutrients.

Implications for Immunotherapy

Most approved cancer immunotherapies work by targeting killer T cells directly, yet only about 20 to 40 percent of patients respond. Bolstering the dendritic cells that train and activate those T cells could bring the benefits of immunotherapy to more patients.

The UCLA team also tested creatine's effects on human dendritic cells. Creatine treatment enhanced the activation of human monocyte-derived dendritic cells — the type commonly used in dendritic cell cancer vaccines — and improved their ability to stimulate T cells against a cancer-associated target.

"The potential we see here is that creatine could be used in two complementary ways: as a supplement to enhance the immune response of patients already receiving immunotherapy, and as a tool to improve the quality of dendritic cell-based vaccines before they're administered," said James Elsten-Brown, a co-first author and graduate student in Yang's lab.

Important Caveats

The researchers emphasized that the study was conducted in cells and mice, not patients, and no dietary or medical recommendations should be drawn from it. Although creatine monohydrate has been widely used as a supplement for decades and is generally considered safe at recommended doses, anyone undergoing cancer treatment should consult their doctor before adding any supplement.

Population-based research has previously reported an association between higher dietary creatine intake and lower cancer incidence, but establishing causation requires clinical trials. The UCLA team plans to collaborate with physicians on prospective clinical trials testing whether creatine supplementation improves outcomes in patients receiving immunotherapy.

The experimental strategies described in the study have not been tested in humans or approved by the FDA. A patent application has been filed by the UCLA Technology Development Group.
